reading.identification: Later-18th/early-19th-century painted-stucco refront on an older narrow-plot Ghent burgher house, Jan Breydelstraat, now a ground-floor interiors/linen shop with dwelling above.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE SPLIT. Set A (aerial tiles) is degraded to unusable — narrow-street photogrammetry collapse, no roof form recoverable. Everything roof-related is inferred. Set B photo 0 is the load-bearing evidence: it resolves shopfront, render, window subdivision and sills at close range. Photo 1 locates the building in its run but I cannot certainly disambiguate the target from its left neighbour there, so storey count stays inferred.

STOREYS. Marked inferred, not seen. Photo 0's outline has a dashed top edge cutting above the first-floor heads, so at least one storey continues out of frame; 3 total is the reading consistent with height_m 9.0 (3.6 + 2.7 + 2.7 = 9.0). Note height_source is "no-data", so 9.0 m is itself a default — if a real height arrives and exceeds ~10.5 m, revisit as 4 storeys, which is equally common on this street.

BAYS / WINDOWS. Two bays is directly seen: two tall windows on the first floor over a display window + door at ground. Fits 5.7 m frontage with substantial piers. Windows read strongly vertical (~2:1), white-painted frames with visible glazing bars subdividing into a small number of large panes — consistent with the late-classical refront, not with original 17th-c. cross windows. Reveal called shallow rather than deep: jamb shadowing is genuinely visible, but a moulded architrave surround on a rendered wall brings the frame forward of the full masonry thickness, and imagery cannot resolve past the class anyway.

MATERIAL AND THE 1-10 CM REGIME. The wall is painted lime stucco over brick — no exposed brickwork on this facade. Use brick permittivity for the substrate but do NOT give it brick roughness: 1.2 mm RMS for old, hand-floated, patched render, against ~3-8 mm for raked joints. Do not mesh brick relief here; at 1.07 cm wavelength a centimetre-bumpy mesh violates the locally-smooth assumption and produces specular garbage. Ornament, mouldings and render undulation all belong in the roughness/scattering term.

WHERE THE GEOMETRY BUDGET GOES. The ground-floor order is the single most radio-relevant feature and the highest-value explicit geometry on this building: veined marble/scagliola pilasters flanking the display window and door, plus the deep moulded entablature over the shopfront. These are 25-30 cm projections at 3.3 m from the street line — wedges and a shallow corner reflector directly at pedestrian beam height. Model them as facets. Second priority: window reveals and the projecting moulded sills (both >10 cm). Third: the main eaves cornice on the silhouette. Trim set to marble for the pilasters specifically; window surrounds and sills are painted render and can share the wall material.

BALCONIES. False, and this is a seen negative — photo 0 resolves the target's first floor clearly and shows terracotta planters on plain sills. The wrought-iron balconettes visible in photo 1 are on neighbouring facades to the right; do not propagate them onto this building.

CLUTTER — READ THIS BEFORE PLACING ANYTHING. fronting_street has car_access "none" on a sett-paved living_street. NO VEHICLES. This is precisely the failure mode that filled a pedestrian square with a thousand individually-reasonable parked cars. Correct clutter for this frontage is pedestrian retail: A-boards, the ornate black wall-mounted iron lantern visible in photo 0, dark fabric shop awnings (seen on the adjacent units in photo 1, plausible here), a vertical rainwater downpipe at the party line (seen in photo 1), terracotta window boxes on the first-floor sills, and small wall-mounted CCTV/light fittings above the shopfront. Sett paving should carry real surface variation, not a flat plane.

ROOF. Inferred entirely. Ridge called perpendicular to the street despite the straight classical cornice: a 4.5-5.7 m wide by 11 m deep parcel spans naturally front-to-back, and the standard Flemish pattern is an original gable cut back and masked behind an 18th-c. straight cornice. This also yields the correct raking party-wall silhouette when the camera rotates off-axis. If better roof evidence appears, mansard with a street-parallel ridge is the main alternative and is common on this refront type in Ghent.

ATTACHMENT. 4 attached neighbours, 2 street frontages — party walls left and right should be blind. Only the street facade earns this detail budget; the rear and flanks should stay coarse.
